one_liner: Standards-compliant C99 HTML5/CSS/DOM/URL engine; beats libxml2-based bindings on HTML parsing and CSS selector throughput.
what_it_does: Lexbor is a pure-C99, dependency-free set of modules (HTML5 parser, CSS parser/CSSOM/Selectors, DOM, URL, Encoding, Unicode, Punycode) meant to embed in apps or serve as the base of a browser engine. It is not a libxml2 drop-in: it exposes its own C API (e.g. lxb_html_document_parse, DOM interfaces, a separate selectors module) rather than matching libxml2's calling convention. You link individual module libraries (liblexbor-html, liblexbor-css, ...) or generate a single amalgamated header/source file with the bundled single.pl script for a source-drop integration.
how_it_is_fast: Hot scanning loops (tokenizer character search) use a SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) bit-trick, lexbor_swar_seek4, that checks up to 4 target bytes per machine word instead of per-byte comparisons (source/lexbor/core/swar.h, based on the Stanford 'bit twiddling hacks' techniques). Keyword/tag lookups use a compact static binary search tree (lexbor_sbst_entry_static_t, source/lexbor/core/sbst.h) baked in at compile time instead of runtime hashing. Node and string allocation goes through a custom arena/region allocator (mraw) plus fixed-size object pools (dobject), cutting malloc/free call counts versus a generic tree library. The HTML tokenizer itself is a hand-written WHATWG-spec state machine rather than a generic/recursive parser.
when_to_use: High-volume HTML5 parsing of real-world (possibly malformed) markup where a spec-conformant tokenizer matters, e.g. scraping/crawling pipelines (SerpApi runs lexbor in production for this).
Need HTML parsing and CSS selector matching from one dependency-free C library instead of wiring libxml2 plus a separate CSS engine.
Embedding in a size- or dependency-constrained project via the single-header amalgamation (perl single.pl --all), with no libxml2/expat linkage.
Batch/throughput workloads (many documents or many CSS queries per run) where the benchmark shows the gap over libxml2-based bindings widens most.
Already need URL parsing, 40+ text encodings, or Unicode normalization/IDNA alongside HTML/CSS, and want one codebase for all of it.
when_not_to_use: Need XML (non-HTML) parsing, XPath, or XSLT — lexbor targets HTML5/CSS/URL/DOM, not general XML; libxml2 still covers that ground.

Multiple threads touching one parsed document concurrently: the CMake LEXBOR_WITHOUT_THREADS option is documented as inert ('Not used now, for the future'), and no locking is visible in the mraw arena allocator.
Need well-defined reference-counted/GC'd DOM node lifetime across a long-lived app — 'Reference counting of DOM nodes' (issue #132) is still open and unresolved.
Depend on the Layout or Fonts modules — both are marked 'in progress' in the README and are not usable yet.

Writing in Crystal/Ruby/Python/Elixir without going through a wrapper: those bindings (kostya/lexbor, Nokolexbor, Selectolax, fast_html) add their own overhead, and part of the benchmark's largest ratios (51-79x, 116x CSS) come from the baseline's slow Ruby CSS-via-XPath path, not a guaranteed win in every host language.

integration.form: source-drop (single-header amalgamation via single.pl) or static/shared lib via CMake
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler; CMake for building from source (no minimum GCC/Clang version stated in docs)
integration.platforms: prebuilt binaries for x86-64 (CentOS, Debian, Fedora, RHEL, Ubuntu) plus Homebrew/MacPorts on macOS and vcpkg; builds from source on any platform with a C99 compiler and CMake, including Windows via MSYS — other architectures require a source build (README asks to email support for anything beyond x86-64 binaries)
integration.thread_safety: not documented as thread-safe; LEXBOR_WITHOUT_THREADS CMake flag exists but is explicitly inert ('Not used now, for the future'), and no locking is present in the mraw arena allocator
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — own C API, not libxml2-API-compatible; language wrappers (Nokolexbor for Ruby, Selectolax for Python) offer a closer drop-in feel within their own ecosystems, not at the C level

gotchas: DOM node reference counting/lifetime is an open design question (issue #132, still open) — do not assume libxml2-style ownership semantics.
Memory comes from a per-document arena (mraw) plus object pools (dobject); document teardown follows lexbor's own lifecycle calls, not ad hoc free().
Layout and Fonts modules are listed 'in progress' in the README; only DOM, HTML, CSS, URL, Encoding, Unicode, and Punycode are marked ready.

Project policy restricts AI-authored contributions to the core library (README 'AI Policy'): PRs touching core C code that read as AI-generated are likely to be rejected, relevant if you plan to upstream a patch.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Use lexbor directly, in C/C++, when you need HTML+CSS+URL+Encoding together with no dependency; on Python or Ruby, selectolax and Nokolexbor already embed lexbor as a backend, so use those instead of binding lexbor yourself. MyHTML (also lexborisov's) is lexbor's own now-superseded predecessor benchmarked against Gumbo/html5ever — lexbor is its actively developed successor, not a co-equal alternative.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party Crystal-language benchmark (kostya/lexbor, not the lexbor project) parsed a 1.5MB Google search-results HTML page 1000 times and ran 5000 CSS selector queries on a Ryzen 3800x. Same-language comparisons show lexbor beating libxml2-backed bindings by ~3.0x (Crystal Crystagiri) to ~4.6x (Ruby Nokogiri) on parsing and ~51x-79x on CSS selection (Nokogiri's CSS runs through XPath translation); the headline 116x and the 45.6x M1 figures mix Crystal against Ruby or reflect an anomalous Crystal/libxml2 binding path and are not like-for-like.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-22, ~2.1k stars) under Apache-2.0, and easy to vendor via the single-header amalgamation script (single.pl), so treated as 'copyable' usability.
